speaker: Carson Block
title: Carson Block: Building Muddy Waters, Short Selling, Quant Strategies & Market Risk
question: Why does traditional fundamental stock picking for undiscovered value companies struggle to work as expected in modern US equity markets?
guest: Going back to how I grew up and what I learned, the traditional idea was to find these diamonds in the rough, undiscovered companies that have good fundamentals and improving fundamentals, and eventually the market will also find them and you will make money. When you think about how we look at momentum and flows now, we just do not believe the market works that way in the US anymore because there is so much passive money. Really, the company itself is the marginal buyer of its own stock, and if it can buy its stock up enough to squeeze the float and get itself into an index, then it becomes this virtuous cycle of index buying.

points.core: Dominant passive index flows prevent fundamental price discovery from reliably re-rating neglected stocks.
points.note: Accept: heavy passive investing warps price discovery so improving fundamentals alone no longer attract active buyers to close valuation gaps. Do not credit: generic complaints about market efficiency or short-termism.

points.core: Corporations themselves often serve as the marginal buyers via share buybacks.
points.note: Accept: companies repurchasing their own shares drive marginal demand rather than outside fundamental investors. Do not credit: surface mention of capital allocation without identifying the company as marginal buyer.

points.core: Buybacks shrink available float enough to push stocks into major benchmark indices.
points.note: Accept: repurchases squeeze the tradeable float and lift market cap/price toward index eligibility thresholds. Do not credit: generic claims that buybacks boost EPS.

points.core: Entering a major index triggers a self-reinforcing cycle of automatic passive buying.
points.note: Accept: index inclusion creates a virtuous feedback loop of price-insensitive inflows from index funds. Do not credit: vague statements that index funds are popular.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Traditional value picking assumes that if you find a cheap, overlooked company, other investors will eventually notice and bid the price up to fair value. Several features of modern US markets weaken both halves of that assumption.

First, little is truly undiscovered. Regulation FD, instant electronic filings, cheap data, and quantitative screens mean thousands of professionals and algorithms see the same low price-to-book or low P/E stocks simultaneously. What remains cheap is often cheap for a reason, a "value trap" facing structural decline.

Second, the convergence mechanism has weakened. A large share of money now flows through index funds and ETFs that buy by market capitalization regardless of valuation, so fewer active dollars exist to correct mispricings, and flows tend to favor already-large stocks. Mispricings can persist longer than a manager's clients will tolerate.

Third, accounting metrics have lost meaning. Value increasingly comes from intangibles like software, brands, and network effects, which are expensed rather than capitalized, so book value and earnings misstate true worth.

Finally, private equity and extended private ownership capture many small, cheap companies before public investors can.

quotes: A large share of money now flows through index funds and ETFs that buy by market capitalization regardless of valuation, so fewer active dollars exist to correct mispricings
Mispricings can persist longer than a manager's clients will tolerate.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Traditional value stock picking relies on two assumptions that modern US market structure has largely eroded: that genuinely overlooked bargains exist in plain sight, and that other active investors will eventually recognize their intrinsic worth and bid prices up to fair value. Today, ubiquitous financial data, quantitative factor screens, and automated research instantly flag statistical cheapness, meaning few public US companies are truly undiscovered; stocks trading at steep discounts often face secular disruption rather than temporary neglect. More importantly, the mechanism for multiple expansion has weakened as capital has shifted massively from active fundamental managers to price-insensitive passive index funds and short-term, catalyst-focused multi-manager hedge funds. Because passive vehicles allocate by market capitalization rather than valuation, small or out-of-index value stocks lack the deep pool of marginal fundamental buyers needed to drive a re-rating, leaving cheap shares stuck at depressed multiples unless management forces realization through buybacks, dividends, or a sale. Meanwhile, private equity keeps or takes many promising smaller firms off public exchanges, and intangible-heavy business models distort classic book-value accounting metrics.

noweb.answer: Traditional fundamental stock picking for undiscovered value struggles in modern US equity markets because structural shifts have eroded both information asymmetries and the catalysts that correct mispricings. Ubiquitous financial databases, quantitative algorithms, and alternative data instantly screen every public company, leaving almost no genuinely overlooked bargains; statistically cheap stocks today are usually discounted for well-understood secular flaws rather than market neglect. Even when genuine mispricings occur, the dominance of passive, market-cap-weighted index funds allocates capital mechanically to the largest winners regardless of valuation, starving smaller undervalued shares of the active buying pressure needed to close valuation gaps. Meanwhile, deep private equity and venture capital markets keep high-quality emerging businesses private longer or acquire undervalued firms directly, leaving behind an adversely selected public small-cap pool prone to value traps. Finally, modern economic moats rely heavily on intangible assets like software, research, and network effects, which traditional accounting expenses rather than capitalizes on balance sheets, making classic book-value and earnings multiples far less reliable guides to true intrinsic worth.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Traditional stock picking for "undiscovered" value companies works only if two things hold: you can find a mispricing others missed, and other investors later notice and push the price back toward fair value. Both have weakened in US markets.

Finding an edge is much harder now. Filings, data feeds, screening tools and alternative data reach thousands of professional analysts and quant funds almost instantly, so obviously cheap stocks are usually cheap for a reason, such as falling earnings, weak governance or poor capital allocation. Those are value traps. Accounting has also aged badly. Modern firms create most of their value through intangibles like software, brands and R&D, which are expensed, not recorded as assets. That makes book value and P/E poor guides to what a company is worth.

Getting the price to correct is the bigger problem. Passive index funds now hold about half of US fund assets, and they buy by market cap, not by valuation. Money keeps flowing into large index members, while small, overlooked companies can stay cheap for years without a catalyst. Finally, private equity often buys good small companies before public investors find them, which leaves a weaker pool of listed small caps.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Traditional fundamental stock picking for undiscovered value companies struggles in modern US equity markets because the structural conditions that once created easy mispricings have largely eroded. Instant access to financial filings, quantitative screening, and alternative data means thousands of institutional analysts and algorithms rapidly price in public information, leaving very few stocks genuinely overlooked. Meanwhile, the dominance of passive, market-cap-weighted index funds directs capital toward the largest and fastest-growing companies regardless of valuation, depriving cheap, smaller stocks of the buying pressure needed to close valuation gaps. At the same time, the US economy has shifted toward intangible assets like software, brand equity, and network effects. Because accounting rules expense most intangible investments rather than capitalizing them, traditional metrics such as price-to-book often misclassify strong businesses as expensive and structurally declining firms as bargains. Finally, promising companies now stay private far longer through venture capital and private equity, shrinking the public pool of hidden gems while winner-take-most dynamics increasingly favor established growth leaders over cheap laggards.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Traditional value investing depends on finding a company whose future cash flows are worth more than its stock price implies. In modern U.S. markets, widely available filings, cheap data, and competition from institutional and quantitative investors mean that obvious bargains based on public information tend to get noticed quickly.

Among overlooked companies, low valuations often reflect real problems such as deteriorating earnings, heavy debt, weak governance, or thin trading. Price-to-book ratios can also mislead when much of a company’s value comes from software, brands, or other assets that accounting captures poorly. Even when a stock is genuinely undervalued, the gap can persist for years, and trading costs and the opportunity cost of waiting can eat into returns.

The challenge is to identify what the market is misjudging about future cash flows and why that misjudgment is likely to correct. A low multiple alone gives you little evidence of either.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Traditional value stock picking relies on finding a gap between a company’s price and its underlying value before other investors recognize it. In modern US markets, financial filings reach investors simultaneously, and inexpensive screening tools let anyone identify stocks trading at low multiples within seconds. A low price may be easy to spot, but deciding whether it reflects a bargain or a lasting decline in earnings still requires an edge.

Overlooked companies do exist, especially among smaller, thinly traded stocks. Yet trading costs can absorb part of the potential gain, and even a sound valuation offers no timetable for the market to agree. The difficulty is finding a gap large enough to compensate for risk, costs, and the time it may take to close.
